_readme: Simulated annotator perspectives (V-054, D-017).
WHY THESE EXIST. Our self-consistency passes used to be the SAME model,
same prompt, at temperature 0.0 — a near-deterministic sample repeated.
The literature is blunt about this: at T=0 self-consistency is
meaningless, because the second sample carries no new information. Since
the agreement score between passes is this product's ONLY confidence
signal (D-006), that made the signal close to decorative.
The fix is NOT temperature noise and NOT a multi-model jury. Raising
temperature buys diversity by degrading each individual judgement, and
panel research shows nine frontier judges collapse to ~2.2 effective
independent votes because their errors correlate — the single best judge
matched or beat the full panel on every dataset tested.
Instead these condition ONE model on genuinely different reading
stances, the way a real defense panel differs: one examiner wants the
requirement demonstrated in the text, another credits substance that is
present but imperfectly worded. Disagreement between them is real
information about the manuscript being borderline — exactly what should
reach the instructor — rather than sampling jitter.
These are DATA, not code (ground rule 7): an instructor may reasonably
disagree with how a stance is worded, and changing one must never need a
code change. Changing ANY text here changes what the agreement score
means, so it is a measurement change: bump semantic_grading's
prompt_version and re-run the golden harness (TESTING §2).
Order matters — `passes` are taken in listed order, and `tie_break` is
spent only when the first two disagree (D-011's quota rule).

perspectives.label: Evidence-first reader
perspectives.stance: You are the examiner who asks to be SHOWN. A criterion is satisfied only if specific text in this document demonstrates it. Where the document gestures at a requirement without actually carrying it out, say so plainly. Do not credit intent, and do not fill gaps with what a capstone of this kind usually contains.

perspectives.label: Charitable reader
perspectives.stance: You are the examiner who reads for substance. Students often satisfy a requirement in their own words, out of the expected order, or under a different heading — credit that when the text genuinely does the work, even if the wording is clumsy or the terminology is non-standard. Do not credit something that is merely implied or absent.

perspectives.label: Adjudicator
perspectives.stance: Two examiners disagreed on this criterion. Weigh only what the document text can support: decide whether the requirement is genuinely demonstrated in the text, or whether the case for it depends on assumption. If the evidence is genuinely balanced, say so rather than forcing a confident verdict.
